newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Bulgaria told conditions must be right for EU aid.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria told conditions must be right for EU aid.

text.p: Bulgarian President Petar Stoyanov was left in no doubt on Thursday that Sofia must put its political house in order before there could be any chance of EU-led assistance to pull it out of its dire economic crisis.
A day after raising the prospect of Bulgaria defaulting on its external debt he met European Commissioners on Thursday in a bid to secure EU help.
"Bulgarian people did not expect me to return with a bag full of miracles," he told a news conference as he approached the end of his first official visit abroad since taking over the presidency.

A sympathetic European Commission told him the political conditions in his country must be right before the 15-nation bloc would initiate an international effort to provide more economic aid to stop the country collapsing.

"The European Commission stated that, as soon as the political situation in Bulgaria allows it, it would consider taking the necessary initiatives to mobilise support for Bulgaria from the international financial institutions and the world community...," the Commission said in a statement.

The EU's External Relations Commissioner, Hans van den Broek, said political parties in Bulgaria must resolve their differences and agree on early elections to create a situation where economic reforms would succeed.

Asked, after he and Commission President Jacques Santer met Stoyanev, if the EU was prepared to go it alone with new aid, he said it was important that Bulgaria saw "eye to eye" with the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
On Wednesday, Stoyanov warned that Bulgaria faced financial collapse and might have to default on debt repayments due later this year to avoid a social explosion.

Appealing for Western help to overcome the economic crisis, Stoyanov said Bulgaria had not received proper recognition for its sacrifices in complying with international economic embargoes against former Yugoslavia and Iraq.
Stoyanov, a pro-market liberal who took office last week, laid much of the blame for the country's dire economic problems at the door of the ruling ex-communist Socialists.
Stoyanov, whose country is mired in strikes and rallies, said "unpredictable social consequences" would follow if the economic crisis was worsened by meeting international debt obligations.
Bulgaria is one of 10 eastern European countries that have applied for EU membership, but is thought unlikely to be among the first group with which the bloc is expected to open talks next year.

Stoyanov told reporters after meeting the European commissioners that although he realised his country would not be in the EU's first round of expansion talks, a protracted delay would make Bulgarians lose faith in the exercise.
After failing to find a compromise between warring political factions, Stoyanov on Tuesday asked Nikolai Dobrev, the interior minister of the Socialist party, to form a new government.

Under the constitution, Stoyanov had to give the mandate to the Socialists -- parliament's biggest party and the caretaker government since Socialist prime minister Zhan Videnov resigned on December 21.
The Socialists rejected his call for them to return the mandate and agree to fresh elections.
